questions.q: Which of the following does NOT survive a SQL Server service restart?
options: User objects, temp tables, and version-store rows in tempdb used for snapshot isolation
Server-level login credentials
The instance's backup and restore history
Server-wide configuration settings like max server memory
questions.explain: tempdb is rebuilt from scratch every time the instance starts, so anything in it — temp tables, table variables, and version-store rows used for snapshot isolation — is gone after a restart, unlike logins, backup history, or sp_configure settings which persist in the other system databases.

questions.q: Which DMV shows currently executing requests along with their wait_type and wait_time_ms?
options: sys.dm_exec_sessions
sys.dm_exec_requests
sys.dm_exec_connections
sys.dm_os_wait_stats
questions.explain: sys.dm_exec_requests returns one row per currently executing request, including its wait_type and wait_time_ms; sys.dm_os_wait_stats is a cumulative, instance-wide aggregate rather than a per-request snapshot.

questions.q: Which DMV would you query to see per-database I/O stall time broken out separately for data files and log files?
options: sys.dm_exec_query_stats
sys.dm_os_performance_counters
sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats
sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
questions.explain: sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats reports read/write counts and cumulative I/O stall time for every database file, letting a DBA see whether I/O pressure is concentrated on data files, log files, or tempdb.

questions.q: Which column in sys.dm_exec_requests identifies the session that is currently blocking a given request?
options: wait_resource
session_id
wait_type
blocking_session_id
questions.explain: blocking_session_id holds the SPID of the session holding the lock the current request is waiting on; a value of 0 means the request isn't blocked at all.

questions.q: Which dynamic management function reports an index's average fragmentation percentage and page count?
options: sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats
sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
sys.indexes
sys.dm_db_index_operational_stats
questions.explain: sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats scans or samples an index's pages and returns avg_fragmentation_in_percent along with page counts, which is the standard basis for rebuild-vs-reorganize decisions.

questions.q: How should a DBA treat the suggestions returned by sys.dm_db_missing_index_details?
options: As a definitive list of indexes that must be created immediately
As a suggestion based on compiled query plans since the last restart — not a guaranteed performance win
As a list of indexes that are corrupted and need repair
As a record of every index that has ever been dropped from the database
questions.explain: Missing-index DMVs only accumulate from plans compiled since the last restart, don't account for existing similar indexes or write overhead, and reset on restart — so they're a starting point for investigation, not an automatic action list.

questions.q: Which DMV lists currently active transactions in the instance along with their start time?
options: sys.dm_exec_sessions
sys.dm_os_wait_stats
sys.dm_tran_active_transactions
sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
questions.explain: sys.dm_tran_active_transactions returns one row per active transaction in the instance, including transaction_begin_time, which is essential for finding long-running transactions that are holding locks or preventing log truncation.

questions.q: Under READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT isolation, what happens when a reader accesses a row that's currently being modified by an uncommitted transaction?
options: It always sees the uncommitted new value immediately
It blocks until the writer's transaction commits or rolls back
It raises a deadlock error immediately
It reads a versioned "before" image of the row from the tempdb version store instead of blocking
questions.explain: RCSI uses row versioning stored in tempdb so a reader gets a transactionally consistent snapshot of the row as it existed before the write began, avoiding the blocking behavior of default READ COMMITTED.

questions.q: What's required before BACKUP LOG can be used against a database?
options: The database must be in FULL or BULK_LOGGED recovery model — SIMPLE recovery truncates the log and doesn't support log backups
BACKUP LOG works under any recovery model, including SIMPLE
RESTORE LOG must be run first to enable log backups
The database must be set to read-only
questions.explain: Log backups only make sense under FULL or BULK_LOGGED recovery, where the log is retained for point-in-time recovery; under SIMPLE recovery the log is truncated on checkpoint and BACKUP LOG is not a supported operation.

questions.q: After restoring a full backup, which RESTORE option leaves the database in a restoring state so a differential or log backup can still be applied?
options: WITH RECOVERY
WITH NORECOVERY
WITH STANDBY
WITH CHECKSUM
questions.explain: WITH NORECOVERY keeps the database in a restoring state, ready to accept further differential or log restores; WITH RECOVERY rolls back uncommitted transactions and brings the database fully online, ending the restore sequence.

questions.q: What defines an "orphaned user" in a SQL Server database?
options: A login with no server role assigned
A user account that has been disabled by the DBA
A database user whose SID doesn't match any server-level login's SID — often after restoring to a different instance
A user who has never connected to the database
questions.explain: Orphaning happens when a database is restored or attached to an instance where the matching login (by SID) doesn't exist, breaking the mapping between the database user and any server login; it's commonly fixed with ALTER USER ... WITH LOGIN or sp_change_users_login.

questions.q: If a user is granted SELECT on a table through a role, but also has an explicit DENY SELECT applied directly, what's the effective permission?
options: GRANT always overrides DENY
The most recently applied permission wins, regardless of type
DENY only applies to server-level principals, not database users
DENY overrides any GRANT the user has, whether direct or inherited through role membership
questions.explain: DENY is the strongest permission state in SQL Server's authorization model — it overrides any GRANT the principal holds from any source, including role membership, so the user ends up unable to SELECT.

questions.q: For a SQL Server Agent alert to actually notify a DBA when it fires, what's required?
options: An operator configured and linked to the alert, with Database Mail set up to send the notification
Nothing — alerts notify automatically with no additional configuration
Alerts can only be reviewed later in the SQL Server error log
The instance must be restarted before the alert takes effect
questions.explain: An alert on its own only detects a condition; it needs an operator (who to notify) linked to it and a working Database Mail profile for the actual email/page to go out.

questions.q: Which msdb object is the authoritative source for the outcome, duration, and message of every SQL Server Agent job step execution?
options: msdb.dbo.sysjobs
msdb.dbo.sysjobhistory
sys.dm_exec_requests
master.dbo.sysprocesses
questions.explain: sysjobs only stores the job's definition; sysjobhistory is the table that actually records each step's run outcome, duration, and any message text every time the job executes.

questions.q: What does DBCC CHECKDB actually validate when run against a database?
options: Only index fragmentation levels
Only whether all configured logins still exist
Logical and physical consistency of the database's allocation structures and objects
Only the size of the transaction log
questions.explain: DBCC CHECKDB checks allocation consistency across the whole database plus the structural and logical integrity of every table and index, catching corruption that could otherwise sit undetected until a query fails or a page-level error occurs.

questions.q: Why is setting a data file's autogrowth to a small fixed increment (e.g., 1 MB) problematic on a heavily-written database?
options: It has no measurable impact on a busy database
It permanently disables instant file initialization
It causes the transaction log to shrink automatically
Frequent small autogrowth events cause repeated growth overhead and file fragmentation under write-heavy load
questions.explain: Each autogrowth event pauses writes while SQL Server extends the file; tiny increments mean this happens constantly under sustained writes, adding overhead and scattering the file's physical layout — much worse than sizing files appropriately up front.

questions.q: What does Query Store retain that the default plan cache does not?
options: Historical runtime statistics and plan history that persist across restarts and plan cache evictions
Only the single most recent execution plan per query
Login audit history for compliance purposes
Index fragmentation history over time
questions.explain: The plan cache is volatile and cleared by restarts, memory pressure, and plan eviction; Query Store persists compiled plans and their runtime statistics to disk, letting a DBA look back at how a query performed days or weeks earlier.

questions.q: A stored procedure runs fast for one parameter value but very slow for another, even though the query text and WHERE clause never change. What's the most likely cause?
options: A syntax error that only manifests with certain parameter values
Parameter sniffing — the cached plan was compiled and optimized for a parameter value whose data distribution differs sharply from the current call
TempDB has run out of space
The procedure needs to be recompiled by renaming it
questions.explain: SQL Server compiles a plan using the parameter values present the first time the procedure runs (or after a recompile); if that value's row distribution is atypical, the resulting plan can be badly suited to other parameter values, producing wildly different runtimes.

questions.q: When building reusable DBA scripts for a personal toolkit, why parameterize thresholds like fragmentation percentage or free-space percentage instead of hardcoding them?
options: Parameters make T-SQL scripts run measurably slower
Hardcoding thresholds is required by SQL Server's security model
Hardcoded thresholds require editing the script for every server or environment; parameters make one script reusable across many contexts
SQL Server does not allow variables inside maintenance scripts
questions.explain: A script with hardcoded thresholds only fits the one server it was written for; exposing thresholds as parameters (or configuration values) lets the same script run correctly across development, staging, and production environments with different workloads.

questions.q: Why should a DBA toolkit script log its own execution history to a table rather than only printing output to the SSMS results pane?
options: PRINT output is preserved permanently in msdb by default
Logging automatically resolves any problems the script finds
SQL Server requires all maintenance scripts to log to a table by policy
A logged history table lets you track trends over time and prove the script actually ran on schedule, since PRINT output disappears once the session ends
questions.explain: Once an SSMS session closes, any PRINT output is gone; writing results to a persistent log table gives a durable audit trail for proving a script ran, comparing results over time, and building alerting on top of it.
